```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5

```

envirolipids predicts Net Primary Productivity (NPP) from brGDGTs. The workflow is the same for modern
samples and for paleo records, but the results are presented differently:

* **modern data** are a set of separate samples, plotted **by sample**;
* **paleo data** are a sequence through time, plotted **against age**.

This vignette works through one example of each. Every step is a separate
function that returns an object: `print()` shows the results as a table and
`autoplot()` plots them. By default `autoplot()` plots by sample. Passing a
numeric `x` (such as age) plots a series instead.

```{r}
library(envirolipids)
```

# Input data

Data need one column per brGDGT compound (`fIa`, `fIb`, `fIc`, `fIIa`, `fIIa_`,
`fIIb`, `fIIb_`, `fIIc`, `fIIc_`, `fIIIa`, `fIIIa_`, `fIIIb`, `fIIIb_`,
`fIIIc`, `fIIIc_`), given either as fractions (summing to 1) or as percentages
(summing to 100). Columns are matched by name, so their order does not matter.
An `ID` column, if present, is used to label the samples. Any other columns
are ignored.

# Modern data: plotting by sample

## The data

`modern_example_data` contains 20 modern samples (soils, lake sediments and
peats) from sites around the world. Abundances are given as percentages. Each
sample also has its observed NPP.

```{r}
data(modern_example_data)
head(modern_example_data[, c("ID", "Sampletype", "Latitude", "Longitude",
                             "NPP")])
```

These samples are a subset of the data used to train the NPP model, so they
also illustrate how well the model reproduces the NPP it was trained on.
Predictions for genuinely new samples will be less accurate.

## Describe the samples

Summarising brGDGTs by methylation group gives a quick overview of the
compositions:

```{r}
modern_methylation <- brgdgt_methylation(modern_example_data)
head(modern_methylation)
```

## Check applicability

Before predicting NPP, check whether the samples fall within the brGDGT
composition space of the training data:

```{r}
modern_check <- npp_brgdgt_applicable(modern_example_data)
modern_check
```

A sample is within the domain if it is no further from the centre of the
training data (Mahalanobis distance) than 99% of the training samples; the
`threshold` argument changes this proportion. The `p_value` column gives the
proportion of training samples at least as far out as each sample.

The per-sample table is available with `as.data.frame(modern_check)`, and the
nearest training samples for each sample with `modern_check$neighbours`.

```{r, fig.cap = "Mahalanobis distance of each sample to the training data"}
autoplot(modern_check, type = "mahalanobis")
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Samples on the principal components of the training data"}
autoplot(modern_check, type = "pca")
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Methylation groups (training data sized by NPP)"}
autoplot(modern_check, type = "ternary")
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Training sites with the most similar brGDGT composition", eval = requireNamespace("maps", quietly = TRUE)}
autoplot(modern_check, type = "map")
```

## Predict NPP from brGDGTs

The samples are of different types, so `sample_type` is given per sample:

```{r}
modern_npp <- npp_brgdgt(modern_example_data,
                         sample_type = modern_example_data$Sampletype)
head(modern_npp)
```

```{r, fig.cap = "brGDGT-based NPP for each sample, with 95% intervals"}
autoplot(modern_npp)
```

For modern samples, the predictions can be compared with observed NPP:

```{r, fig.cap = "Predicted vs observed NPP; the dashed line is the 1:1 line"}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data.frame(observed = modern_example_data$NPP,
                  predicted = modern_npp$estimate,
                  lower = modern_npp$lower, upper = modern_npp$upper),
       aes(x = observed, y = predicted)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Observed NPP (gC m-2 yr-1)", y = "Predicted NPP (gC m-2 yr-1)") +
  theme_minimal()
```


# Paleo data: plotting through time

## The data

`example_data` contains 50 samples from a sediment core, with ages in years
BP. Abundances are given as fractions.

```{r}
data(example_data)
head(example_data)
```

## Describe the samples

```{r}
paleo_methylation <- brgdgt_methylation(example_data)
summary(paleo_methylation[, c("tetra", "penta", "hexa")])
```

## Check applicability

The check is the same as for modern data. Plotting against age shows whether
particular periods fall outside the training data.

```{r}
paleo_check <- npp_brgdgt_applicable(example_data)
paleo_check
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Mahalanobis distance to the training data through time"}
autoplot(paleo_check, type = "mahalanobis", x = example_data$Age,
         xlab = "Age (years BP)")
```

The PCA, ternary and map plots do not have a time axis, and work as for modern
data:

```{r, fig.cap = "Core samples on the principal components of the training data"}
autoplot(paleo_check, type = "pca")
```

## Predict NPP from brGDGTs

All samples come from lake sediments:

```{r}
paleo_npp <- npp_brgdgt(example_data, sample_type = "Lacustrine Sediment")
head(paleo_npp)
```

```{r, fig.cap = "brGDGT-based NPP through time, with 95% interval"}
autoplot(paleo_npp, x = example_data$Age, xlab = "Age (years BP)")
```

```{r}
sessionInfo()
```
